knowledge_point.title: Integrating an Algebraic Function With Negative Integer Exponent

question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we rewrite the integral as

$$
\int 3(5-3x)^{-3}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=5-3x.$ Then differentiating with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-3\,⟹\,\text{d}x=-\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u.
$$

We now write our integral in terms of $u,$ calculate the integral as normal, and write the final answer in terms of $x$ at the very end:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 3(5-3x)^{-3}\,\text{d}x & =3\int {u}^{-3}\cdot (-\frac{1}{3})\,\text{d}u \\  & =3\cdot (-\frac{1}{3})\int {u}^{-3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\int {u}^{-3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{(-2)}{u}^{-2}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(5-3x)^{-2}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2(5-3x)^{2}}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Let's double-check that our result is correct. If we differentiate the result, then it should come out to the original integrand:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[\frac{1}{2(5-3x)^{2}}+C] & =\frac{1}{2}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[\frac{1}{(5-3x)^{2}}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[(5-3x)^{-2}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot (-2)(5-3x)^{-3}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(5-3x)+0 \\  & =-(5-3x)^{-3}\cdot (-3) \\  & =3(5-3x)^{-3} \\  & =\frac{3}{(5-3x)^{3}}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Integrating an Algebraic Function With Negative Integer Exponent

question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we rewrite the integral as

$$
\int 4(3-x)^{-5}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=3-x.$ Then differentiating with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=-\text{d}u.
$$

We now write our integral in terms of $u,$ calculate the integral as normal, and write the final answer in terms of $x$ at the very end:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 4(3-x)^{-5}\,\text{d}x & =4\int {u}^{-5}\cdot (-1)\,\text{d}u \\  & =4\cdot (-1)\int {u}^{-5}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-4\int {u}^{-5}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-4\cdot \frac{1}{(-4)}{u}^{-4}+C \\  & =(3-x)^{-4}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{(3-x)^{4}}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Let's double-check that our result is correct. If we differentiate the result, then it should come out to the original integrand:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[\frac{1}{(3-x)^{4}}+C] & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[\frac{1}{(3-x)^{4}}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[(3-x)^{-4}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\  & =(-4)(3-x)^{-5}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3-x)+0 \\  & =(-4)(3-x)^{-5}\cdot (-1) \\  & =4(3-x)^{-5} \\  & =\frac{4}{(3-x)^{5}}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$
